The core innovation lies in transforming sample-only generative models into calibrated predictive distributions using randomized probability integral transforms (PIT). Starting from m Monte Carlo draws per input x, the method first applies an affine bias correction to align the generator's output with observed data characteristics. Then, a randomized PIT is computed on the calibration split, where each draw gets mapped to a uniform value based on its rank among the m draws. This creates a discrete uniform distribution over {1/(N+1), ..., N/(N+1)}, which is then inverted via a conformal calibration map Ĉ_m to yield a calibrated predictive CDF. The resulting distribution supports arbitrary queries such as exceedance probabilities, quantiles, and tail losses. Optional Gaussian smoothing improves robustness by reducing variance in low-density regions. Theoretical guarantees include finite-sample uniform calibration and marginal coverage bounds. However, this approach assumes exchangeability across calibration/test sets and does not provide conditional coverage, limiting its applicability in dynamic environments.
